coupling-element.summary: The flexible members that transmit torque between the hubs and the spacer while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement between the shafts.
coupling-element.function: The flexible members that transmit torque between the hubs and the spacer while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement between the shafts.
coupling-element.operatingPrinciple: Each flexible plane allows a small angle between the parts on either side of it. With a spacer coupling there are two flexible planes, one at each end of the spacer, so a parallel offset between the shafts is taken up as a small angle at each plane, and angular misalignment is shared between them. Depending on type, flexibility comes from deforming an elastomer, flexing thin metal discs, sliding of crowned gear teeth, or flexing of a spring-steel grid.
coupling-element.construction: Elastomeric types (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) use rubber or polyurethane elements and give some damping. Disc couplings use laminated packs of thin stainless steel discs bolted alternately to hub and spacer flanges, need no lubrication, and have limited misalignment capacity and a definite axial stiffness. Gear couplings use crowned external teeth in internal sleeve teeth, carry high torque for their size, and need lubrication. Grid couplings use a tapered spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, need lubrication and give some damping.

motor-stator.summary: The stationary electromagnetic part of the motor.
motor-stator.function: The stationary electromagnetic part of the motor. When its three-phase winding is connected to an alternating supply, it produces a magnetic field that rotates at synchronous speed.

The field induces currents in the rotor cage, and their interaction with the field produces torque.

bearing-de.summary: Carries the radial load at the coupling end of the rotor (its share of the impeller's hydraulic radial force, the rotor weight and any loads from the coupling) while letting the shaft expand axially.

The inner ring rotates with the shaft and is clamped against a shaft shoulder by the locknut and lockwasher. The outer ring is stationary and has a fit in the housing bore that allows it to slide, with axial clearance left at the covers. When the shaft lengthens relative to the casing as it warms, the whole bearing moves with the shaft and the outer ring slides in the bore. This is the 'floating' bearing; the axial position of the rotor is set by the locating bearing at the non-drive end.

The inner ring sees a rotating load (the load direction moves round it as it turns), which is why it needs an interference fit on the shaft; the outer ring sees a stationary load, which allows the looser fit needed for floating.

grout.function: Fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation, spreading the load evenly, bonding the baseplate to the foundation so that they act as one stiff structure, adding damping and protecting the underside of the baseplate from moisture.
grout.operatingPrinciple: Properly placed grout makes full, void-free contact with both the baseplate and the foundation, so static and dynamic loads pass into the concrete over a large area instead of through a few points. This greatly increases the effective stiffness of the baseplate and raises the natural frequencies of the installed unit.

impeller-1.summary: Closed radial impeller of stage 1; adds energy to the liquid.
impeller-1.function: Adds energy to the liquid in stage 1. Each impeller in the series raises the pressure by roughly the same amount, so the pump head is about the number of stages times the head per stage. The first stage sees the lowest inlet pressure and therefore governs the NPSH required by the pump; some designs use a special first-stage impeller with a larger eye or a separate inducer / booster stage.
impeller-1.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters the eye axially, the rotating vanes turn it outward and accelerate it. Energy from the shaft appears as a pressure rise inside the impeller and as high absolute velocity at the outlet, which the diffuser then converts into pressure. Head per stage depends mainly on the tip speed (u2 = pi * D2 * n / 60): roughly proportional to D2 squared and n squared (affinity laws).
impeller-1.construction: Closed impeller: hub and back shroud, front shroud with the eye and a wear-ring land, and backward-curved vanes cast between them (shown with 6 vanes, illustrative). In this model all impellers face the suction (drive) end and are keyed to the shaft, separated by interstage sleeves and clamped as a stack by shaft nuts. Many pumps use identical impellers in every stage; the first stage may differ.

keyConcepts.title: Why several impellers
keyConcepts.body: Head per stage is limited by tip speed and by the impeller proportions that give good efficiency at a given flow. Putting n identical stages in series multiplies the head (H ~ n * H_stage) at the same flow.

keyConcepts.title: Specific speed per stage
keyConcepts.body: For a multistage pump, specific speed is calculated with the head per stage, not the total head: n_q = n * sqrt(Q) / H_stage^0.75.

assumptions: Vane number, angles and proportions are illustrative. Some designs use a double-suction first stage or opposed impellers.

diffuser-1.summary: Stationary vaned diffuser around the stage 1 impeller; converts velocity into pressure.
diffuser-1.function: Collects the fast-moving liquid leaving impeller 1 and slows it down in widening vane channels, converting kinetic energy into static pressure. In the last stage of any build, the diffuser discharges into the discharge casing instead of a return channel.
diffuser-1.operatingPrinciple: The flow leaves the impeller with a large tangential velocity. The diffuser vanes form channels whose area grows in the flow direction; by continuity the velocity falls and, by energy conservation (Bernoulli), static pressure rises. Because the vanes surround the whole impeller symmetrically, the radial hydraulic force on the impeller is small compared with a single volute.
diffuser-1.construction: Front wall, vane ring and a diaphragm (separating wall) cast or machined as one part, located in the stage casing by a spigot / shoulder. In many designs the diffuser vanes and the return vanes are one casting on either side of the diaphragm; in others the return channel is part of the stage casing. The diaphragm hub carries a renewable interstage bush around the interstage sleeve.

keyConcepts.title: Diffuser vs volute
keyConcepts.body: A volute (spiral casing) suits single-stage pumps; diffusers with return channels are compact and give a nearly balanced radial load, which is why ring-section multistage pumps use them.

return-channel-1.summary: Guide vanes leading the flow from diffuser 1 to the eye of impeller 2.
return-channel-1.function: Turns the flow leaving diffuser 1 through 180 degrees around the diaphragm and guides it radially inward to the eye of impeller 2, removing most of the swirl so that the next impeller receives an even, nearly swirl-free inflow.

return-channel-1.construction: Back wall with return vanes and a nose that carries the casing wear ring of the next stage. In many designs it is cast together with the diffuser (diaphragm between them) or forms part of the stage casing.

impeller-2.summary: Closed radial impeller of stage 2; adds energy to the liquid.
impeller-2.function: Adds energy to the liquid in stage 2. Each impeller in the series raises the pressure by roughly the same amount, so the pump head is about the number of stages times the head per stage.
impeller-2.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters the eye axially, the rotating vanes turn it outward and accelerate it. Energy from the shaft appears as a pressure rise inside the impeller and as high absolute velocity at the outlet, which the diffuser then converts into pressure. Head per stage depends mainly on the tip speed (u2 = pi * D2 * n / 60): roughly proportional to D2 squared and n squared (affinity laws).
impeller-2.construction: Closed impeller: hub and back shroud, front shroud with the eye and a wear-ring land, and backward-curved vanes cast between them (shown with 6 vanes, illustrative). In this model all impellers face the suction (drive) end and are keyed to the shaft, separated by interstage sleeves and clamped as a stack by shaft nuts. Many pumps use identical impellers in every stage; the first stage may differ.

keyConcepts.title: Why several impellers
keyConcepts.body: Head per stage is limited by tip speed and by the impeller proportions that give good efficiency at a given flow. Putting n identical stages in series multiplies the head (H ~ n * H_stage) at the same flow.

keyConcepts.title: Specific speed per stage
keyConcepts.body: For a multistage pump, specific speed is calculated with the head per stage, not the total head: n_q = n * sqrt(Q) / H_stage^0.75.

diffuser-2.summary: Stationary vaned diffuser around the stage 2 impeller; converts velocity into pressure.
diffuser-2.function: Collects the fast-moving liquid leaving impeller 2 and slows it down in widening vane channels, converting kinetic energy into static pressure. In the last stage of any build, the diffuser discharges into the discharge casing instead of a return channel.
diffuser-2.operatingPrinciple: The flow leaves the impeller with a large tangential velocity. The diffuser vanes form channels whose area grows in the flow direction; by continuity the velocity falls and, by energy conservation (Bernoulli), static pressure rises. Because the vanes surround the whole impeller symmetrically, the radial hydraulic force on the impeller is small compared with a single volute.
diffuser-2.construction: Front wall, vane ring and a diaphragm (separating wall) cast or machined as one part, located in the stage casing by a spigot / shoulder. In many designs the diffuser vanes and the return vanes are one casting on either side of the diaphragm; in others the return channel is part of the stage casing. The diaphragm hub carries a renewable interstage bush around the interstage sleeve.

impeller-3.summary: Closed radial impeller of stage 3; adds energy to the liquid.
impeller-3.function: Adds energy to the liquid in stage 3. Each impeller in the series raises the pressure by roughly the same amount, so the pump head is about the number of stages times the head per stage.

diffuser-3.summary: Stationary vaned diffuser around the stage 3 impeller; converts velocity into pressure.
diffuser-3.function: Collects the fast-moving liquid leaving impeller 3 and slows it down in widening vane channels, converting kinetic energy into static pressure. In the last stage of any build, the diffuser discharges into the discharge casing instead of a return channel.
diffuser-3.operatingPrinciple: The flow leaves the impeller with a large tangential velocity. The diffuser vanes form channels whose area grows in the flow direction; by continuity the velocity falls and, by energy conservation (Bernoulli), static pressure rises. Because the vanes surround the whole impeller symmetrically, the radial hydraulic force on the impeller is small compared with a single volute.
diffuser-3.construction: Front wall, vane ring and a diaphragm (separating wall) cast or machined as one part, located in the stage casing by a spigot / shoulder. In many designs the diffuser vanes and the return vanes are one casting on either side of the diaphragm; in others the return channel is part of the stage casing. The diaphragm hub carries a renewable interstage bush around the interstage sleeve.

impeller-5.summary: Closed radial impeller of stage 5; adds energy to the liquid.
impeller-5.function: Adds energy to the liquid in stage 5. Each impeller in the series raises the pressure by roughly the same amount, so the pump head is about the number of stages times the head per stage.
impeller-5.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters the eye axially, the rotating vanes turn it outward and accelerate it. Energy from the shaft appears as a pressure rise inside the impeller and as high absolute velocity at the outlet, which the diffuser then converts into pressure. Head per stage depends mainly on the tip speed (u2 = pi * D2 * n / 60): roughly proportional to D2 squared and n squared (affinity laws).
impeller-5.construction: Closed impeller: hub and back shroud, front shroud with the eye and a wear-ring land, and backward-curved vanes cast between them (shown with 6 vanes, illustrative). In this model all impellers face the suction (drive) end and are keyed to the shaft, separated by interstage sleeves and clamped as a stack by shaft nuts. Many pumps use identical impellers in every stage; the first stage may differ.

keyConcepts.title: Why several impellers
keyConcepts.body: Head per stage is limited by tip speed and by the impeller proportions that give good efficiency at a given flow. Putting n identical stages in series multiplies the head (H ~ n * H_stage) at the same flow.

keyConcepts.title: Specific speed per stage
keyConcepts.body: For a multistage pump, specific speed is calculated with the head per stage, not the total head: n_q = n * sqrt(Q) / H_stage^0.75.

assumptions: Vane number, angles and proportions are illustrative. Some designs use a double-suction first stage or opposed impellers.

diffuser-5.summary: Stationary vaned diffuser around the stage 5 impeller; converts velocity into pressure.
diffuser-5.function: Collects the fast-moving liquid leaving impeller 5 and slows it down in widening vane channels, converting kinetic energy into static pressure. In the last stage of any build, the diffuser discharges into the discharge casing instead of a return channel.
diffuser-5.operatingPrinciple: The flow leaves the impeller with a large tangential velocity. The diffuser vanes form channels whose area grows in the flow direction; by continuity the velocity falls and, by energy conservation (Bernoulli), static pressure rises. Because the vanes surround the whole impeller symmetrically, the radial hydraulic force on the impeller is small compared with a single volute.
diffuser-5.construction: Front wall, vane ring and a diaphragm (separating wall) cast or machined as one part, located in the stage casing by a spigot / shoulder. In many designs the diffuser vanes and the return vanes are one casting on either side of the diaphragm; in others the return channel is part of the stage casing. The diaphragm hub carries a renewable interstage bush around the interstage sleeve.

impeller-6.summary: Closed radial impeller of stage 6; adds energy to the liquid.
impeller-6.function: Adds energy to the liquid in stage 6. Each impeller in the series raises the pressure by roughly the same amount, so the pump head is about the number of stages times the head per stage.

Energy from the shaft appears as a pressure rise inside the impeller and as high absolute velocity at the outlet, which the diffuser then converts into pressure. Head per stage depends mainly on the tip speed (u2 = pi * D2 * n / 60): roughly proportional to D2 squared and n squared (affinity laws).
impeller-6.construction: Closed impeller: hub and back shroud, front shroud with the eye and a wear-ring land, and backward-curved vanes cast between them (shown with 6 vanes, illustrative). keyConcepts.title: Why several impellers
keyConcepts.body: Head per stage is limited by tip speed and by the impeller proportions that give good efficiency at a given flow. Putting n identical stages in series multiplies the head (H ~ n * H_stage) at the same flow.

keyConcepts.title: Specific speed per stage
keyConcepts.body: For a multistage pump, specific speed is calculated with the head per stage, not the total head: n_q = n * sqrt(Q) / H_stage^0.75.

diffuser-6.summary: Stationary vaned diffuser around the stage 6 impeller; converts velocity into pressure.
diffuser-6.function: Collects the fast-moving liquid leaving impeller 6 and slows it down in widening vane channels, converting kinetic energy into static pressure. When this is the last stage (6-stage build) it discharges into the discharge casing.
diffuser-6.operatingPrinciple: The flow leaves the impeller with a large tangential velocity. The diffuser vanes form channels whose area grows in the flow direction; by continuity the velocity falls and, by energy conservation (Bernoulli), static pressure rises. Because the vanes surround the whole impeller symmetrically, the radial hydraulic force on the impeller is small compared with a single volute.
diffuser-6.construction: Front wall, vane ring and a diaphragm (separating wall) cast or machined as one part, located in the stage casing by a spigot / shoulder. In many designs the diffuser vanes and the return vanes are one casting on either side of the diaphragm; in others the return channel is part of the stage casing. The diaphragm hub carries a renewable interstage bush around the interstage sleeve.

balance-drum.summary: Rotating drum behind the last impeller that counteracts most of the axial thrust.
balance-drum.function: Balances most of the axial thrust of the impellers. The remaining (residual) thrust in either direction is carried by the thrust bearing at the non-drive end.
balance-drum.operatingPrinciple: The impeller side of the drum is at (nearly) discharge pressure; the balance chamber behind it is connected to suction by the leak-off line. The pressure difference acting on the drum face area produces a force toward the discharge end, opposite to the impeller thrust. A controlled leakage flows through the narrow radial gap between drum and bush; the drum force does not adjust itself to changes in thrust, so a thrust bearing is required.
balance-drum.construction: Sleeve-like drum keyed or shrunk on the shaft, running in a stationary drum bush with a small radial clearance. Its diameter is chosen by the designer from the expected thrust.

balance-disc.summary: Rotating disc that balances the axial thrust automatically by adjusting an axial gap.
balance-disc.function: Balances the whole axial thrust of the impellers in most operating conditions, so a separate thrust bearing is usually not needed; the rotor floats axially.
balance-disc.operatingPrinciple: Liquid at discharge pressure passes a radial throttle gap and then the axial gap between disc and seat into the balance chamber (connected to suction). If the rotor moves toward suction, the axial gap closes, the pressure on the disc rises and pushes the rotor back; if it moves the other way, the gap opens and the force falls. The disc therefore finds an equilibrium position automatically.
