curves.disclaimer: ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Generated from generic curve shapes for teaching (4 stages x an assumed stage curve). Not manufacturer test data, not a rating and not suitable for pump selection or design. Use the OEM curve for the actual pump, stage count and impeller diameter.
curves.source: Generated in code: H = 4 x H_stage,bep (1.22 - 0.06 q - 0.16 q^2), eta = eta_bep (2q - q^2), P = rho g Q H / eta, NPSHr = NPSHr_bep (0.6 + 0.4 q^3), q = Q / Q_bep.
assumptions: All values are illustrative, chosen for teaching only.
Head of the whole pump is shown as 4 x the stage head; real stages differ slightly (first stage, last stage, leakage).
The minimum continuous stable flow and the allowable region come from the manufacturer; 40 % of BEP flow is an example only.
Balance leak-off and interstage leakage are included implicitly in the assumed efficiency.

engineering.note: Example inputs for a generic 4-stage ring-section pump (70 m per stage) - illustrative, not a rating.

whyMultistage.title: Why several impellers in series?
whyMultistage.body:
The head one impeller can produce is set mainly by its tip speed: H is roughly proportional to (D2 x n)^2. To reach a high head with one impeller you would need a very large diameter or a very high speed. A large, narrow impeller at moderate flow has high disc-friction and leakage losses (low specific speed, low efficiency), and very high speeds bring mechanical and NPSH limits.

Putting several moderate impellers in series on one shaft multiplies the head: the same flow passes every stage and each adds its share, so H_total ~ n_stages x H_stage while the flow stays the same. Each stage can then run at a specific speed that gives good efficiency.

This is different from several separate pumps: a multistage pump is one machine with one shaft, one pair of bearings, two shaft seals and one driver. Pumps connected in series in a pipeline add heads in the same way, but each has its own casing, seals and driver.
keyPoints: Series stages: flow is the same, heads add.
Parallel pumps: head is the same, flows add.
Specific speed of a multistage pump uses the head per stage.

pressureProgression.explanation: Set by the suction system; must give enough NPSH available for the first stage.

pressureProgression.pressure: Rises inside the impeller, high velocity at the outlet
pressureProgression.explanation: Energy is added as pressure and kinetic energy.

pressureProgression.pressure: Static pressure rises further, velocity falls
pressureProgression.explanation: Kinetic energy is converted into pressure; some is lost in the crossover and return channel.

pressureProgression.pressure: Each stage adds roughly the same pressure rise
pressureProgression.explanation: Pressure grows almost linearly with stage number at a given flow.
About suction pressure + n x stage pressure rise, minus small losses.
Connected to suction by the leak-off line; this keeps the NDE seal at low pressure.

topics.title: Axial thrust in a multistage pump
topics.body: Each closed impeller has a net axial force toward its suction eye: the back shroud is exposed to outlet pressure over a larger area than the front shroud (whose eye area sees suction pressure of that stage), and the incoming flow is turned through 90 degrees (momentum). In an in-line ring-section pump all impellers face the same direction, so the stage forces add up. The total can be large and changes with flow, clearance wear and suction pressure.
keyPoints: Forces add up when impellers face the same way.
Thrust changes with flow rate, wear-ring and bush clearances and suction pressure.
It must be balanced hydraulically and the remainder carried by a bearing (or a disc).

topics.title: Hydraulic balancing methods
topics.body:
Methods: (1) balance drum (piston) plus a thrust bearing; (2) balance disc that adjusts its own axial gap; (3) drum-and-disc combinations; (4) opposed (back-to-back) impeller arrangements, where two groups of impellers face each other and their thrusts largely cancel - common in axially split and barrel pumps; (5) balance holes and back wear rings on individual impellers (more common in single-stage pumps).

Manufacturers choose differently because they weigh different risks: a drum has no rubbing faces and is robust in transients but needs a thrust bearing and leaks more; a disc balances automatically and saves the thrust bearing but can rub at start-up, shut-down and with dirty liquids; opposed impellers need crossover passages and a longer, more complex casing. Liquid cleanliness, temperature, start-stop frequency, required efficiency and the company’s design tradition all play a part.
topics.caution: No balancing device removes the need to check the actual design: the residual thrust, its direction and the bearing arrangement are OEM-specific.

topics.title: How the balance drum and the balance disc work
topics.body:
Drum: the drum behind the last impeller sees discharge pressure on its front and balance-chamber pressure (about suction) on its back. Force = pressure difference x drum face area, directed toward the discharge end. Leakage through the narrow radial gap returns to suction through the leak-off line. The force does not adjust itself, so the residual thrust goes to the thrust bearing.

Disc: liquid passes a radial throttle gap and then the axial gap between the rotating disc and its seat. If the rotor moves toward suction, the axial gap narrows, the pressure in front of the disc rises and pushes the rotor back; if it moves the other way the gap opens and the pressure falls. The rotor settles where the disc force equals the impeller thrust - automatically, at every operating point.
keyPoints: Drum: fixed geometry, predictable leakage, needs a thrust bearing.
Disc: self-adjusting gap, usually no thrust bearing, sensitive at start-up/shut-down and to solids.
Both need a free, unblocked leak-off line.

topics.title: Interstage leakage and wear-ring clearances
topics.body: Each stage has internal leakage paths: from the impeller outlet back to its eye across the casing wear ring, and from stage to stage across the interstage bush. Leakage rises with clearance and differential pressure. As clearances wear, the pump delivers less head and flow for the same power, efficiency falls, the axial thrust changes and the rotor loses part of the support the annular seals give (stiffness and damping), so vibration can rise. Many users trend head, power and balance leak-off to decide when to renew clearances.
topics.caution: New and maximum clearances are design values from the OEM; do not apply rules of thumb from other pumps.

topics.title: Shaft deflection and critical speed
topics.body: The shaft of a multistage pump is long and slender compared with a single-stage pump. Static deflection (weight, radial hydraulic load) must stay well inside the annular clearances. The rotor also has natural bending frequencies; operating close to the first one gives large vibration. In a dry rotor these are the "dry" critical speeds; in operation, the liquid in the wear rings, interstage bushes and balance drum acts like additional bearings (Lomakin effect) and raises and damps them. When clearances wear, this support falls - one reason why worn multistage pumps vibrate more. Designers keep stage count, bearing span and shaft diameter in proportion; very long pumps may be split into two pumps or built with opposed impellers and a centre bush.

topics.title: Bearing arrangements
topics.body: Drum design: a radial bearing at one end and a locating thrust bearing (often paired angular-contact ball bearings, or a tilting-pad thrust bearing in large pumps) at the other carry the residual thrust and fix the rotor position. Disc design: the disc positions the rotor, so both bearings must allow axial movement (e.g. cylindrical roller or sleeve bearings). Lubrication is usually oil bath with constant-level oilers, ring oil or forced oil in larger pumps; grease in smaller ones.

topics.title: Mechanical seal systems
topics.body: Both seals of a ring-section pump with a balance device normally run close to suction pressure, which allows standard seals even for high discharge pressures. The seal environment is set by a piping plan: flush from discharge or from the balance chamber, cooling for hot water, quench, or a buffer / barrier system for hazardous liquids. In boiler feed service, seal cooling or a cooled flush is common because the water is hot. Vent the seal chambers before start-up.

topics.title: NPSH and cavitation
topics.body: Only the first stage sees low inlet pressure, so it governs NPSH required. NPSH available = (p_suction,abs - p_vapour) / (rho g) + v^2 / (2 g) at the suction nozzle reference plane. NPSH3 (the published NPSHr) is defined at a 3 % head drop of the first stage, so cavitation is already present at NPSHr; a margin is needed (see ANSI/HI 9.6.1 and the OEM). Hot feedwater has a high vapour pressure, so boiler feed pumps usually take suction from a deaerator placed well above the pump, or use a booster pump.
topics.caution: A test or catalogue NPSHr is not a safe operating limit on its own; use the manufacturer’s margin recommendations.

topics.title: Multistage pump efficiency
topics.body: Each stage has hydraulic losses (impeller, diffuser, crossover and return channel), volumetric losses (wear rings, interstage bushes, balance leak-off) and mechanical losses (disc friction, bearings, seals). The balance leak-off is a loss specific to balanced multistage pumps. Efficiency is highest at the best efficiency point (BEP) and falls away from it; clearance wear lowers it over time. Because the stages are in series, the stage efficiency largely sets the pump efficiency, apart from fixed bearing / seal losses.

topics.title: Minimum continuous stable flow
topics.body: At low flow, most of the shaft power turns into heat in a small amount of liquid, the temperature rises and can approach vapour pressure (especially with hot feedwater), recirculation forms at the impeller inlet and outlet, and axial and radial forces become unsteady. Manufacturers state a minimum continuous stable flow (and a thermal minimum flow). An automatic recirculation valve or a minimum-flow line back to the suction vessel protects the pump when the system demand is low.
topics.caution: Never run a multistage pump against a closed discharge valve longer than the OEM allows.

topics.title: Other multistage configurations (not modelled here)
topics.body: Barrel-type (double-casing) pumps: a forged barrel encloses an inner casing (ring sections or axially split) and is closed by a high-pressure cover; used for very high pressures and temperatures such as large boiler feed. Axially split multistage pumps: the casing is split horizontally through the shaft centreline, often with opposed impellers; the rotor can be lifted out after removing the upper half; used for pipelines, water injection and large flows. Vertical multistage (in-line) pumps and submersible borehole pumps use the same series-stage principle with different casings.
topics.caution: These are different designs. This 3D model shows only the ring-section (segmental) type.

families.name: Grey cast iron
families.description: An iron-carbon-silicon casting alloy in which most of the carbon is present as graphite flakes. The flakes give excellent castability, machinability and vibration damping, but they act as internal notches, so grey iron has low ductility and low toughness compared with ductile iron or steel. It is the traditional, economical material for casings, bearing housings and some baseplates in clean-water service.
families.mechanicalStrength: Good compressive strength but limited tensile strength and very little elongation. Because the graphite flakes concentrate stress, the material is brittle and can fracture with little warning under impact, shock, overpressure, water hammer, excessive pipe loads or uneven bolt loads. Properties vary with section thickness and cooling rate, so different sections of a heavy casting may not have identical strength.
families.corrosionResistance: Similar to other unalloyed irons: rusts in aerated water, is generally acceptable in clean, near-neutral water, and is limited in seawater, acidic or otherwise aggressive water unless coated or protected. Long exposure to some waters causes graphitic corrosion, a selective loss of iron that leaves a weak graphite-rich network which may not be obvious from the surface.
families.wearResistance: Fair sliding behaviour because graphite acts as a solid lubricant, but grey iron is not normally used as a wear-ring or sleeve material against hard counterfaces.
families.abrasionResistance: Low to moderate. Erodes readily in water carrying hard solids, especially in high-velocity zones such as the volute tongue, the impeller inlet region and around wear-ring clearances.
families.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for ambient and moderately elevated water temperatures. Sensitive to thermal shock and rapid temperature change. The allowable pressure-temperature combinations are set by the applicable casting and pump standards and the OEM design, not by the material family alone.
families.costConsiderations: Usually the lowest-cost casting material for pump casings, widely available from foundries, with established pattern equipment for many standard pump ranges.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Excellent fluidity and castability allow complex suction and volute passages; very good machinability. Weld repair is difficult and is frequently restricted or prohibited on pressure-containing parts; where permitted it needs preheat, suitable consumables and an approved procedure. A stress-relief heat treatment may be applied for dimensional stability before final machining of the split joint and bores.
advantages: Excellent castability for complex hydraulic passages
Adequate corrosion behaviour in clean, near-neutral water
limitations: Brittle: low ductility and impact resistance because of the graphite flakes
Weld repair is difficult and often not permitted on pressure parts
Limited resistance to seawater, acidic or aggressive water
Susceptible to graphitic corrosion over long service
Excluded by many process-industry specifications for flammable or hazardous liquids
suitableService: Cooling water in treated or closed systems
Irrigation and fire water where the governing specification allows it

families.name: Ductile (spheroidal graphite) iron
families.description: Cast iron in which the graphite is present as spheroids (nodules) rather than flakes, achieved by treating the molten iron, typically with magnesium, before casting. Nodular graphite does not act as a sharp notch, so ductile iron keeps much of the castability of grey iron while offering significantly higher strength, ductility and toughness.
families.mechanicalStrength: Higher tensile strength, elongation and impact toughness than grey iron, giving much better tolerance of overpressure, water hammer, nozzle loads and handling impacts. The grade (ferritic, pearlitic or mixed matrix), nodularity and section size determine the actual properties, which should be confirmed from the material certificate.
families.corrosionResistance: Broadly similar to grey iron: rusts in aerated water, acceptable in clean near-neutral water, and limited in seawater and acidic media without protection. Internal coatings are often applied to extend life in water service.
families.wearResistance: Fair for sliding contact, similar to grey iron. Not normally used for wear rings without surface treatment.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate. Somewhat better than grey iron because of its toughness, but it still erodes in high-velocity, solids-laden flow.
families.temperatureSuitability: Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures, with better thermal-shock tolerance than grey iron. Low-temperature impact toughness depends on the grade. Pressure-temperature limits come from the applicable standards and the OEM design.
families.costConsiderations: Moderately more expensive than grey iron because of the nodularising treatment and tighter process control; usually well below cast steel and stainless steels.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Good castability, although it shows a greater shrinkage tendency than grey iron and needs careful feeding and metallurgical control to maintain nodularity. Good machinability. Weld repair is possible with qualified procedures but can alter the microstructure near the weld, so repairs on pressure parts need OEM and specification approval. Heat treatment can be used to adjust the matrix and properties.
advantages: Much greater ductility and toughness than grey iron
Higher strength allows lighter or higher-pressure casings
Better tolerance of pipe loads, water hammer and handling impact
Cost remains well below steel and stainless alloys
limitations: Corrosion resistance broadly similar to grey iron
Properties depend on nodularity and must be verified
Weld repair requires qualified procedures and approval
Not suitable for seawater or acidic service without protection
suitableService: Municipal and potable water, with approved coatings where required
Cooling water and general industrial water
Fire protection pumping where the specification allows it
Higher-pressure water service where grey iron is not acceptable

families.name: Cast carbon steel
families.description: Steel castings with low to moderate carbon content and no significant alloying additions. Cast steel is chosen for pressure-containing parts when higher strength, toughness and weldability than cast iron are required, for example at higher pressures or temperatures, or where specifications exclude cast iron for flammable or hazardous liquids.
families.mechanicalStrength: High strength and toughness with good ductility; tolerates pressure transients and external loads well. Low-temperature toughness depends on composition and heat treatment and is verified by impact testing where required.
families.corrosionResistance: Limited. Rusts in water and lacks the graphite-rich surface layer that helps cast iron in some waters, so designs typically include a corrosion allowance and may be coated. Not suitable for seawater or corrosive chemicals without protection.
families.wearResistance: Moderate. Not used as a wear-ring or sleeve material without surface hardening or overlay.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate. Tougher than cast iron but of similar hardness, so erosion still occurs in solids-laden flow; extra wall thickness or liners are used where wear is expected.
families.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for higher temperatures than cast iron within the pressure-temperature ratings of the applicable standard. Low-temperature duties need impact-tested material.
families.costConsiderations: Higher than cast iron because of higher pouring temperatures, more feeding metal, heat treatment and inspection; usually below stainless and duplex alloys.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: More demanding to cast than iron: higher pouring temperature, greater shrinkage and a greater tendency to casting defects, so castings are commonly inspected by non-destructive testing and repaired by welding under qualified procedures. Normally heat treated (for example normalised) after casting. Good weldability and machinability.
advantages: Weldable, so casting defects can be repaired under qualified procedures
Accepted by many higher-pressure and hazardous-fluid specifications
Better thermal-shock tolerance than cast iron
limitations: Poor corrosion resistance in water without coating or corrosion allowance
More expensive and slower to produce than iron castings
Castability inferior to cast iron for thin, complex passages
Requires heat treatment and inspection
suitableService: Hot water duties within the applicable ratings
Hydrocarbon or hazardous liquids where cast iron is excluded
typicalUse: Casing nozzles as part of the casing casting

families.name: Cast austenitic stainless steel
families.description: Cast chromium-nickel stainless steels, with or without molybdenum, for example compositions related to the molybdenum-bearing 316-type family. Cast grades have their own designations and often contain some ferrite in their microstructure, so they should not be treated as identical to wrought grades. Corrosion resistance comes from a thin, self-repairing chromium-rich passive film.
families.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength with good ductility and toughness, including at low temperatures. Strength is lower than that of duplex stainless steels and cannot be increased by heat treatment.
families.corrosionResistance: Good general corrosion resistance in many waters and chemicals. Susceptible to pitting and crevice corrosion in chloride-containing water, especially where flow is stagnant, temperature is raised, or oxidisers such as chlorine are present; molybdenum-bearing grades perform better than molybdenum-free grades. Chloride stress corrosion cracking is possible at elevated temperatures.
families.wearResistance: Moderate. Austenitic stainless steels have a strong tendency to gall when rubbing against similar stainless alloys, which matters at wear rings and threaded parts.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate. Better than cast iron where corrosion and erosion act together, but not a wear-resistant material for heavy solids.
families.temperatureSuitability: Wide range from low to elevated temperatures within code ratings. The risk of chloride stress corrosion cracking increases with temperature.
families.costConsiderations: Significantly higher than cast iron; sensitive to nickel and molybdenum market prices.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Good castability with appropriate foundry practice; solution heat treatment after casting is normally applied to restore full corrosion resistance. Weldable with qualified procedures. Machining is slower than for iron because the material work-hardens, so tooling and cutting parameters must suit it.
advantages: Weldable and repairable under qualified procedures
Suitable for potable and high-purity duties where approved
No rust contamination of the pumped liquid
limitations: Pitting and crevice corrosion in chloride environments
Chloride stress corrosion cracking at elevated temperature
Galling tendency in stainless-on-stainless sliding contact
Lower strength than duplex alloys
Higher cost than cast iron
suitableService: Many dilute chemical solutions, subject to corrosion data
Brackish water only after careful assessment of chlorides and temperature
typicalUse: Casing halves for corrosive or high-purity service

families.name: Duplex stainless steel
families.description: Stainless steels with a mixed ferritic-austenitic microstructure, generally higher in chromium than common austenitic grades and alloyed with molybdenum and nitrogen. The two-phase structure gives substantially higher strength than austenitic stainless steels and improved resistance to chloride pitting, crevice corrosion and stress corrosion cracking. Available as castings for casings and impellers and as wrought bar for shafts and sleeves.
families.mechanicalStrength: Substantially higher strength than austenitic stainless steels with good toughness, which supports stiff, compact shafts and good fatigue performance. Toughness depends on a correct ferrite-austenite balance and the absence of embrittling phases.
families.corrosionResistance: Better chloride pitting and crevice corrosion resistance than common austenitic grades and much better resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking. The Pitting Resistance Equivalent Number (PREN) is a calculated index based on chromium, molybdenum and nitrogen content, with molybdenum and nitrogen weighted more heavily than chromium. It is used to rank alloys comparatively; several formula variants exist, and PREN alone does not predict performance in a specific fluid, temperature or crevice geometry.
families.wearResistance: Moderate to good; harder than austenitic grades, but galling is still possible against similar alloys, so wear-ring pairs need attention.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate to good where corrosion and erosion act together, generally better than austenitic grades; not a substitute for hard wear materials in heavy slurries.
families.temperatureSuitability: Good from low to moderately elevated temperatures. Prolonged exposure in an intermediate elevated temperature range causes embrittlement, which limits the upper service temperature; the limit is set by the applicable codes and material supplier.
families.costConsiderations: Typically higher than austenitic stainless castings, although higher strength can reduce section sizes. Fewer foundries are qualified, which can affect lead time.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Casting and welding require close control of chemistry, cooling rate and solution annealing to achieve the correct phase balance and to avoid intermetallic phases (such as sigma phase) that reduce toughness and corrosion resistance. Weld repairs need qualified procedures and often ferrite measurement and corrosion testing. Machinability is lower than that of austenitic grades.
advantages: High strength allows compact, stiff designs
Improved resistance to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion
High resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking
One alloy family can cover casing, impeller, shaft and sleeves
limitations: Sensitive to incorrect heat treatment and welding (intermetallic phases)
Upper service temperature limited by embrittlement
Fewer qualified foundries and longer lead times
Still susceptible to crevice corrosion in warm, chlorinated or stagnant seawater
More difficult to machine than austenitic grades
suitableService: Brackish water and many seawater duties after assessment
Desalination and reverse osmosis feed pumping
Mildly acidic or chemical service, subject to corrosion data

families.name: Super duplex stainless steel
families.description: Highly alloyed duplex stainless steels with higher chromium, molybdenum and nitrogen than standard duplex grades. This gives a higher PREN as a comparative index and stronger resistance to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion. Commonly considered for seawater, brines and other aggressive chloride service.
families.mechanicalStrength: Very high strength for a stainless steel with good toughness when correctly heat treated; generally comparable to or above standard duplex grades.
families.corrosionResistance: One of the most resistant stainless steel families in chloride environments, with high resistance to pitting, crevice corrosion and stress corrosion cracking. It is not immune: crevice corrosion can still occur in warm, chlorinated or stagnant seawater, under deposits and in tight crevices, so design details and operating practice still matter.
families.wearResistance: Good; harder than austenitic grades, but galling precautions are still needed for sliding pairs.
families.abrasionResistance: Good resistance to erosion-corrosion in clean or lightly laden seawater; not a slurry material.
families.temperatureSuitability: As for standard duplex grades: suitable from low to moderately elevated temperatures, with an upper limit set by embrittlement and code rules.
families.costConsiderations: High; one of the more expensive pump alloy families, with limited foundry sources and longer lead times.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Even more sensitive than standard duplex to intermetallic phase formation during casting, heat treatment and welding, and heavy sections are difficult to cool quickly enough. Qualified procedures, solution annealing and testing (for example microstructure and corrosion tests) are commonly specified. Machining is demanding.
advantages: High resistance to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion
Good resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking
Avoids the velocity limits of copper alloys in seawater
Long life in seawater when correctly specified and manufactured
limitations: High material and manufacturing cost
Very sensitive to casting, heat treatment and welding quality
Limited foundry capability for large castings
Not immune to crevice corrosion in severe conditions
Accelerates galvanic corrosion of less noble metals coupled to it
suitableService: Seawater intake, cooling and fire water
Reverse osmosis high-pressure and brine duties

families.name: Tin bronze and gunmetal (low-zinc copper alloys)
families.description: Copper-tin casting alloys, including leaded and zinc-containing gunmetal variants, long used for water pump impellers, wear rings and small parts. Because they contain little or no zinc, they resist dezincification, the selective leaching of zinc that weakens high-zinc brasses in many waters. Where brass-type alloys are considered for water service, dezincification-resistant compositions are normally required.
families.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength and good ductility; adequate for impellers and wear rings at moderate peripheral speeds, but lower than steels and stainless steels.
families.corrosionResistance: Good resistance to fresh water and many treated waters and, in suitable compositions, to seawater at moderate velocities. Susceptible to erosion-corrosion at high local velocities, to stress corrosion cracking in the presence of ammonia, and to attack in sulphide-polluted water and some oxidising chemicals.
families.wearResistance: Good sliding and anti-galling behaviour, which makes bronze a common wear-ring partner against stainless steel or against a bronze of different hardness.
families.abrasionResistance: Low to moderate; soft relative to sand and other hard particles, so it erodes in solids-laden water.
families.temperatureSuitability: Ambient to moderately elevated water temperatures; strength reduces as temperature rises.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate to high and sensitive to copper and tin prices; scrap value is high.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Very good castability for impellers and rings and excellent machinability, especially in leaded grades. Weld repair of leaded grades is difficult. Lead content may be restricted by drinking-water regulations, so low-lead or lead-free alloys with national approvals may be required for potable water.
advantages: Good corrosion resistance in fresh water
Good anti-galling behaviour as a wear-ring material
Long, well-documented service history in water pumps
limitations: Limited strength at high peripheral speeds
Erosion-corrosion at high local velocity
Attacked by ammonia, sulphides and some chemicals
Lead content may conflict with potable water rules
Galvanic interaction with iron and steel parts must be considered
suitableService: Municipal and potable water (with approved alloys)
Seawater at moderate velocity in suitable compositions, after assessment
typicalUse: Shaft sleeves in older or low-duty water pumps

families.name: Aluminium bronze (including nickel-aluminium bronze)
families.description: Copper-aluminium alloys, usually with iron and often nickel additions. They combine higher strength than tin bronzes with good resistance to seawater corrosion and cavitation erosion, and are widely used for seawater pump impellers, casings and wear parts. Behaviour varies significantly between grades and heat-treatment conditions, so the specific grade matters.
families.mechanicalStrength: High strength and good toughness for a copper alloy, with good fatigue resistance in seawater.
families.corrosionResistance: Good resistance to seawater and brackish water, with a velocity tolerance generally better than tin bronze, although velocity limits still apply. Some grades and heat-treatment conditions are susceptible to selective phase corrosion (de-aluminification), particularly in crevices, under deposits and in stagnant or polluted seawater, so grade, heat treatment and design detail must address it. Not suitable for many acids, ammonia or sulphide-polluted water.
families.wearResistance: Good; often used for wear rings, though pairings with stainless steel still need attention to galling and hardness difference.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate; better than tin bronze, but still limited in sandy or slurry flows.
families.temperatureSuitability: Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures typical of seawater and cooling duties.
families.costConsiderations: High and sensitive to copper and nickel prices.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Castable, but more demanding than tin bronze because of oxide film and dross formation, so good foundry practice is essential. Weldable with qualified procedures; a post-weld heat treatment may be specified to restore resistance to selective phase corrosion. Machinability is moderate.
advantages: High strength for a copper alloy
Some natural resistance to marine biofouling
limitations: Selective phase corrosion in some grades and conditions
Velocity limits still apply
Sensitive to sulphide-polluted seawater
Galvanic effects when coupled to stainless steel or carbon steel
Higher foundry complexity than tin bronze
suitableService: Fire water drawn from the sea
typicalUse: Casing halves in some seawater designs
Shaft sleeves in some marine designs

families.name: Wrought carbon steel
families.description: Hot-rolled, cold-drawn or forged plain carbon steels, from low-carbon grades to medium-carbon grades that can be hardened. Used for shafts in non-corrosive service where sleeves protect the wetted length, and for keys, coupling hubs, levelling screws, anchor bolts and general fasteners.
families.mechanicalStrength: Moderate to good strength depending on carbon content and heat treatment; good fatigue performance when stress raisers such as keyways and shoulders are well designed and finished.
families.corrosionResistance: Poor in water: rusts readily. Wetted shaft surfaces are normally protected by sealed sleeves, and external surfaces by coatings or lubricant films.
families.wearResistance: Moderate; can be surface hardened (for example by induction hardening) where wear resistance is needed.
families.abrasionResistance: Low to moderate.
families.temperatureSuitability: Satisfactory over the temperature range of most water pumping duties; low-temperature toughness depends on grade.
families.costConsiderations: Low and widely available.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Excellent machinability and availability as bar. Low-carbon grades weld easily; medium-carbon grades need preheat and controlled procedures. Normalising or quenching and tempering adjusts strength.
advantages: Adequate strength for many shafts and hubs
limitations: Poor corrosion resistance
Requires sleeves or coatings where wetted
Lower fatigue strength than alloy steels
Corrosion at keyways and journals reduces fatigue life
suitableService: Clean water where the shaft is fully sleeved

families.name: Low-alloy steel (quenched and tempered)
families.description: Steels with chromium and molybdenum and sometimes nickel additions (for example the 4140-type chromium-molybdenum family, given only as an illustration) that are hardened and tempered to high strength and toughness. Used for highly loaded shafts, casing joint studs and nuts, and coupling components.
families.mechanicalStrength: High strength and fatigue resistance after quenching and tempering, with good toughness when the heat treatment is controlled.
families.corrosionResistance: Similar to carbon steel; requires protection in wetted areas and in corrosive atmospheres. High hardness combined with hydrogen or sour (hydrogen sulphide) environments can cause environmental cracking, so hardness limits are specified for such service.
families.wearResistance: Good when hardened; journals and seats can be surface hardened.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate when hardened.
families.temperatureSuitability: Retains strength at moderately elevated temperatures better than carbon steel. Bolting grades for elevated temperature are specified by the relevant bolting standards.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate; higher than carbon steel because of alloying and heat treatment.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Good machinability in the annealed or quenched and tempered condition. Welding is difficult: preheat, low-hydrogen practice and post-weld heat treatment are needed, and weld repair of shafts is not normally accepted without OEM approval. Heat treatment response depends on section size.
advantages: Allows smaller shaft diameters for the same torque
limitations: Poor corrosion resistance
Difficult to weld or repair
Risk of hydrogen embrittlement and environmental cracking at high hardness
Requires controlled heat treatment
suitableService: Clean water duties with sleeved shafts
Casing bolting in most pump designs

families.name: Martensitic and precipitation-hardening stainless steel
families.description: Stainless steels with enough chromium to form a passive film and a composition balanced so that they can be hardened by heat treatment. The family includes straight-chromium grades (for example 410-type and 420-type), cast martensitic grades with nickel used for impellers, and precipitation-hardening grades. They offer higher strength and hardness than austenitic stainless steels at the expense of some corrosion resistance.
families.mechanicalStrength: High strength and hardness after hardening and tempering, with good fatigue properties. Toughness depends strongly on the tempering treatment.
families.corrosionResistance: Moderate: generally lower than austenitic grades, adequate for fresh water and many mild duties, but prone to pitting in chloride water. Highly hardened conditions are susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement and sulphide stress cracking, so hardness limits apply in sour service.
families.wearResistance: Good. The hardened condition resists galling better than austenitic grades, so martensitic rings are used in wear-ring pairs with a specified hardness differential.
families.abrasionResistance: Good when hardened; used for impellers, rings and sleeves in mildly abrasive water such as sandy river or bore water.
families.temperatureSuitability: Good strength retention at moderately elevated temperatures; suitable grades are used in hot water and condensate duties.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate; usually lower than austenitic or duplex grades of similar form.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Machinable in the annealed or tempered condition; hardened parts may need grinding. Welding requires preheat and post-weld heat treatment to avoid cracking. Heat treatment is essential and must be controlled to balance hardness, toughness and corrosion resistance.
advantages: Better galling resistance than austenitic grades
Good erosion and cavitation resistance in water
Well suited to shafts and sleeves
limitations: Lower corrosion resistance than austenitic grades
Pitting in chloride water
Hydrogen embrittlement and sulphide stress cracking at high hardness
Welding needs strict preheat and post-weld heat treatment
suitableService: Clean and mildly abrasive fresh water
Duties where shaft strength and moderate corrosion resistance are both needed

families.name: Wrought austenitic stainless steel
families.description: Rolled or forged chromium-nickel stainless steels, with or without molybdenum (for example the 304-type and 316-type families, given only as examples). Widely used for shafts, sleeves, wear rings, fasteners, springs and shims where corrosion resistance matters more than high strength.
families.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength in the annealed condition with high ductility and toughness. Cannot be hardened by heat treatment; strength can only be raised by cold work. Lower strength than alloy or martensitic steels, which shaft design must take into account.
families.corrosionResistance: Good general resistance in water and many chemicals; molybdenum-bearing grades have better pitting resistance. Susceptible to pitting and crevice corrosion in chlorides, particularly under gaskets and sleeves and in stagnant zones, and to chloride stress corrosion cracking at elevated temperatures.
families.wearResistance: Poor in self-mated sliding. Stainless-on-stainless contact galls readily (adhesive transfer leading to seizure), which is critical for wear rings, sleeve nut threads and stainless fasteners.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate.
families.temperatureSuitability: Very wide temperature range, including low temperatures; stress corrosion cracking risk in chloride environments increases with temperature.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate to high; sensitive to nickel and molybdenum prices.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Good weldability. Machining is slower than for carbon steel because of work hardening. Solution treatment restores corrosion resistance after hot work where needed. Threaded stainless parts need anti-seize compounds to avoid galling during assembly.
advantages: Good corrosion resistance in water and many chemicals
Readily available as bar, plate, sheet and shim
limitations: Strong galling tendency in sliding contact with itself
Pitting and crevice corrosion in chlorides
Chloride stress corrosion cracking at elevated temperature
Lower strength than alloy or martensitic steels
Cannot be hardened by heat treatment
suitableService: Mild chemical service, subject to corrosion data
typicalUse: Wear rings paired with a dissimilar or harder ring
Fasteners, seal springs and gland plates

families.name: Galling-resistant stainless alloys
families.description: Nitrogen-strengthened austenitic stainless steels with raised manganese and silicon content, developed specifically for resistance to galling and wear in metal-to-metal sliding contact and often sold under proprietary names. They are used where stainless wear-ring pairs, bushings or sleeves would otherwise be at risk of seizure.
families.mechanicalStrength: Higher strength than standard austenitic stainless steels because of nitrogen strengthening, with good ductility.
families.corrosionResistance: Broadly in the range of common austenitic stainless steels in many waters, but performance varies by composition and must be confirmed against the specific fluid, especially in chloride service.
families.wearResistance: Very good galling resistance compared with standard austenitic grades, including against itself and against other stainless steels.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate to good.
families.temperatureSuitability: Good over a wide temperature range, with galling resistance retained at moderately elevated temperatures.
families.costConsiderations: Higher than standard austenitic grades; usually limited to small parts such as rings and bushings.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Machinable with similar precautions to other austenitic stainless steels and weldable with suitable procedures. Usually supplied as bar or ring forgings. Property data must come from the alloy supplier because compositions differ.
advantages: Higher strength than standard austenitic grades
Good corrosion resistance in many waters
Reduces seizure risk at tight running clearances
limitations: Higher cost than standard stainless steel
Corrosion resistance must be confirmed for chloride service
Proprietary compositions vary, so supplier data is essential
Not a substitute for hard materials in abrasive service
suitableService: Clean and corrosive water where stainless rings are required
Duties with a risk of contact at running clearances
Start-up or transient conditions with marginal lubrication

families.name: Engineered polymers and polymer composites
families.description: High-performance thermoplastics and fibre-reinforced polymer composites, for example carbon-fibre-reinforced PEEK-type compounds and filled PTFE compounds. In pumps they are used mainly for stationary wear rings and bushings because they resist galling and seizure, and in some designs as composite coupling spacers or lantern rings.
families.mechanicalStrength: Lower stiffness and strength than metals. Creep under sustained load and temperature must be considered, and rings must be positively retained by the design (interference fit and mechanical locking as specified by the OEM).
families.corrosionResistance: Excellent in water and many chemicals; some compounds are affected by particular solvents, strong acids or oxidisers, so compatibility must be checked for the actual fluid.
families.wearResistance: Good; non-galling against metal counterparts and tolerant of brief contact during start-up or transients.
families.abrasionResistance: Limited to moderate; abrasive solids can wear polymer rings quickly.
families.temperatureSuitability: More limited than metals. Thermal expansion is much higher than that of metals and fluid absorption may cause swelling, both of which change fits and clearances, so the ring design is temperature dependent.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate to high per part.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Machined from moulded stock; dimensional stability, fluid absorption and thermal expansion must be allowed for in the design. Not weldable; damaged parts are replaced.
advantages: Can allow reduced running clearances where the OEM permits
limitations: Temperature limits and high thermal expansion
Creep and retention must be designed for
Limited abrasion resistance
Chemical compatibility must be verified
Any clearance reduction must be OEM approved
suitableService: Duties where seizure risk is high
Upgrades carried out with OEM agreement
typicalUse: Composite coupling spacers in some designs

families.name: Through-hardened bearing steel
families.description: High-carbon chromium steels of very high cleanliness, through-hardened and tempered for rolling contact fatigue resistance, used for the rings and rolling elements of ball and roller bearings. Corrosion-resistant martensitic bearing steels and case-hardened steels are used in special designs. Cages may be pressed steel, machined brass or polymer, depending on bearing design.
families.mechanicalStrength: Very high hardness and rolling contact fatigue strength. Actual bearing life depends on lubrication, load, alignment, fits, temperature and contamination control rather than on the steel alone.
families.corrosionResistance: Poor. Water in the lubricant or condensation in the housing causes corrosion pitting and early failure, so housing seals and lubricant condition are critical.
families.wearResistance: Excellent under correct lubrication.
families.abrasionResistance: Sensitive to particle contamination, which causes indentations and accelerated wear.
families.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for normal bearing operating temperatures; special dimensional stabilisation is used for higher temperatures. In practice the lubricant and cage material usually set the limit.
families.costConsiderations: Bearings are bought-in components; cost depends on bearing type, precision and design rather than on the steel alone.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Produced by specialist bearing manufacturers and not repaired in the field. Mounting requires the fits, heating methods and tools specified by the bearing manufacturer and the pump OEM.
advantages: Long fatigue life when correctly lubricated
limitations: Sensitive to water and particle contamination
Corrodes readily
Susceptible to electrical erosion from stray shaft currents, for example with variable speed drives
Easily damaged by incorrect mounting
suitableService: Rolling bearings in all pump services
Electric motor bearings, with insulated or hybrid designs where current passage is a risk

families.name: Carbon-graphite (seal face grades)
families.description: Mixtures of carbon and graphite that are pressed, baked and usually impregnated with resin or metal to close their porosity. Widely used as the softer face of a mechanical seal pair running against a hard face such as silicon carbide or tungsten carbide. Carbon is self-lubricating, conforms well and tolerates brief marginal lubrication better than hard-on-hard pairs.
families.mechanicalStrength: Low strength and stiffness compared with ceramics and carbides; brittle, so it must be protected from impact, chipping and distortion.
families.corrosionResistance: Carbon itself resists most chemicals. The impregnant (resin or metal) governs compatibility with some solvents, strong oxidisers and alkaline media, and may also affect approvals for drinking water.
families.wearResistance: Good as the soft face of a pair when a stable fluid film exists.
families.abrasionResistance: Poor. Abrasive particles embed in or erode carbon faces, so carbon is avoided in solids-laden liquids unless clean flushing keeps solids away from the faces.
families.temperatureSuitability: Stable over a wide temperature range; oxidising atmospheres at high temperature attack carbon, and resin impregnants have their own limits.
families.costConsiderations: Low to moderate.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded, machined and lapped flat; faces must be handled, stored and installed carefully to avoid chipping and contamination.
advantages: Self-lubricating; tolerant of brief marginal lubrication
Good conformability to the mating face
limitations: Poor abrasion resistance
Brittle and easily chipped
Impregnant may limit chemical compatibility
Blistering can occur in some conditions, for example with viscous liquids
suitableService: Clean water and many clean liquids
Hot water in suitable seal designs
typicalUse: Mechanical seal rotating or stationary face

families.name: Silicon carbide
families.description: A very hard ceramic seal face material with high thermal conductivity. The main types are reaction-bonded silicon carbide, which contains free silicon, and sintered silicon carbide, which does not and therefore has broader chemical resistance. It runs against carbon in clean liquids, or against itself or tungsten carbide where abrasives are present.
families.mechanicalStrength: Very hard and stiff but brittle, with low fracture toughness; sensitive to mechanical impact and, in some grades, to thermal shock.
families.corrosionResistance: Excellent. Sintered grades resist most acids and alkalis; reaction-bonded grades can be attacked by strong alkalis and some acids because of their free silicon phase.
families.wearResistance: Excellent.
families.abrasionResistance: Excellent; preferred in solids-laden service, usually as part of a hard-vs-hard pair with suitable flushing.
families.temperatureSuitability: Very good; high thermal conductivity helps carry frictional heat away from the seal faces.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate to high, depending on grade.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Produced by sintering or reaction bonding, then diamond ground and lapped. Faces can sometimes be relapped within the seal manufacturer limits but cannot otherwise be repaired.
advantages: Very high hardness and abrasion resistance
Broad chemical resistance in sintered grades
limitations: Brittle; sensitive to impact and thermal shock
Hard-vs-hard pairs are very sensitive to dry running and marginal lubrication
Reaction-bonded grades are limited in strong alkalis and some acids
Requires careful handling
suitableService: Abrasive or solids-laden liquids as a hard-vs-hard pair with flushing
typicalUse: Sleeves and bushings in product-lubricated bearings

families.name: Cemented tungsten carbide
families.description: Tungsten carbide particles held in a metallic binder, typically cobalt or nickel. Very hard and tougher than ceramics, it is used as a seal face material where abrasive solids or high pressures are present and as a thermally sprayed coating. Nickel-bound grades are generally preferred in corrosive water because cobalt binder can be leached out.
families.mechanicalStrength: Very hard with higher fracture toughness than silicon carbide; high stiffness and density help faces resist distortion.
families.corrosionResistance: Governed by the binder. The binder can be attacked in acidic or corrosive media, leaving unsupported carbide grains (binder leaching); nickel-bound grades are more corrosion resistant than cobalt-bound grades.
families.wearResistance: Excellent.
families.abrasionResistance: Excellent.
families.temperatureSuitability: Good, though thermal conductivity is lower than silicon carbide; heat checking (surface cracking) can occur under poor lubrication.
families.costConsiderations: High; heavier and generally more expensive than silicon carbide.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Powder metallurgy: pressed, sintered, then ground and lapped. Faces can be relapped within the seal manufacturer limits.
limitations: Binder leaching in corrosive media
High cost and density
Heat checking and dry-running sensitivity in hard-vs-hard pairs
Lower thermal conductivity than silicon carbide
typicalUse: Thermally sprayed coatings on sleeves and rings

families.name: Nitrile rubber (NBR)
families.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene elastomer: a general-purpose O-ring and secondary seal material with good resistance to mineral oils, greases and water at moderate temperatures. Hydrogenated nitrile (HNBR) is a related family with improved heat and ozone resistance.
families.mechanicalStrength: Good tensile strength, tear resistance and compression set for a general-purpose elastomer.
families.corrosionResistance: Good with mineral oils, aliphatic hydrocarbons and water at moderate temperatures. Poor resistance to ozone and weathering, ketones, esters, aromatic and chlorinated solvents, strong acids and oxidisers, and it may degrade over time in chlorinated or chloraminated water.
families.wearResistance: Good for an elastomer.
families.abrasionResistance: Good for an elastomer.
families.temperatureSuitability: Moderate; not suitable for hotter water or steam. Low-temperature flexibility depends on the acrylonitrile content of the compound.
families.costConsiderations: Low.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded and easily compounded. Store away from ozone sources such as electric motors and from sunlight; observe shelf-life guidance from the supplier.
advantages: Good resistance to mineral oils and greases
limitations: Poor ozone and weathering resistance
Limited temperature range
Poor with ketones, esters and aromatic or chlorinated solvents
Limited with oxidisers and some disinfectants

families.name: Ethylene propylene diene rubber (EPDM)
families.description: An elastomer with excellent resistance to water, steam, glycols, ozone and weathering and to many dilute acids and alkalis. Widely used for secondary seals in water services, including potable water where an approved compound is selected.
families.mechanicalStrength: Good general mechanical properties and compression set; peroxide-cured compounds have better heat resistance.
families.corrosionResistance: Excellent with hot water, steam, glycols, ozone and many dilute acids and alkalis. Not compatible with mineral oils, hydrocarbon fuels, petroleum-based greases or many solvents, which cause severe swelling; water, a soap solution or a lubricant approved by the seal supplier should be used during assembly instead of mineral grease.
families.wearResistance: Good for an elastomer.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate to good for an elastomer.
families.temperatureSuitability: Good; suitable for hot water and steam within the limits of the specific compound.
families.costConsiderations: Low.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded. Drinking-water approvals are specific to the compound, not to EPDM in general, and must be confirmed for each part.
advantages: Good resistance to many dilute acids and alkalis
limitations: Swells severely in mineral oils and hydrocarbons
Must not be assembled with petroleum-based greases
Unsuitable for many solvents
Oil contamination of the pumped water can damage seals

families.name: Fluorocarbon rubber (FKM)
families.description: A fluoroelastomer with broad resistance to hydrocarbons, oils, fuels and many acids and chemicals, including at elevated temperatures. Several types exist with different fluorine contents and cure systems, which change both chemical and temperature behaviour, so the grade must be specified, not just the family.
families.mechanicalStrength: Good; typically firmer than NBR and EPDM, with reduced flexibility at low temperatures.
families.corrosionResistance: Excellent resistance to mineral oils, fuels, aromatic hydrocarbons and many acids. Resistance to hot water and steam is limited depending on grade and cure system (some types swell or harden), and resistance to ketones, low-molecular-weight esters, amines and strong alkalis is poor.
families.wearResistance: Good for an elastomer.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate for an elastomer.
families.temperatureSuitability: High temperature capability in air and oils; reduced flexibility at low temperatures. Limits in hot water and steam depend on the grade.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate to high compared with NBR and EPDM.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded; grade selection is critical and should be confirmed with the seal or elastomer supplier.
limitations: Limited in hot water and steam depending on grade
Poor with ketones, amines and some esters
Poor low-temperature flexibility
More expensive than NBR and EPDM
suitableService: Many corrosive chemicals, subject to compatibility data
Water at moderate temperature in suitable grades
typicalUse: Bearing housing lip seals for higher temperatures

families.name: Perfluoroelastomer (FFKM)
families.description: A fully fluorinated elastomer with the widest chemical resistance of the elastomer families, approaching that of PTFE while retaining elasticity. Used where no other elastomer is compatible or where chemistry varies widely.
families.mechanicalStrength: Moderate; some grades show higher compression set and lower resilience than other elastomers, and low-temperature flexibility is limited.
families.corrosionResistance: Very wide chemical resistance, including many acids, alkalis, solvents and oxidisers. Specific grades still have limitations in particular media, such as hot water, steam or amines, so the grade must be checked against the actual fluid.
families.wearResistance: Moderate for an elastomer.
families.abrasionResistance: Moderate for an elastomer.
families.temperatureSuitability: High temperature capability in many media; limited at low temperatures.
families.costConsiderations: Very high; usually justified only where other elastomers are not compatible.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Specialist manufacture with long lead times; parts must be handled carefully. Higher thermal expansion may require groove dimensions specified by the seal manufacturer.
advantages: Widest chemical resistance of the elastomers
One material can cover mixed or variable chemistry
Long life in aggressive service when correctly selected
limitations: Very high cost
Grade-specific chemical limitations still exist
Limited low-temperature flexibility
May need modified groove designs
typicalUse: O-rings and secondary seals in chemical service

families.name: PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene)
families.description: A fluoropolymer that is chemically inert to almost all chemicals and has very low friction. Used in virgin, filled (for example glass, carbon or graphite) or expanded form for gaskets, secondary seal wedges and V-rings, encapsulated O-rings, packing yarns and lantern rings. It is not an elastomer and has little elastic recovery.
families.mechanicalStrength: Low strength and stiffness. PTFE creeps and cold-flows under sustained load, so gaskets can lose bolt load; fillers and expanded structures are used to reduce this.
families.corrosionResistance: Essentially inert to almost all chemicals; only a few highly reactive substances, such as molten alkali metals and elemental fluorine, attack it.
families.wearResistance: Very low friction; virgin PTFE wears quickly, and fillers improve wear resistance.
families.abrasionResistance: Poor in virgin form, improved by fillers.
families.temperatureSuitability: Wide range from very low to elevated temperatures; creep increases with temperature.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Sintered and machined, or skived into sheet; it cannot be moulded like an elastomer. Expanded PTFE is produced by stretching, which improves conformability and creep resistance.
advantages: Approved forms available for food and drinking-water duties
limitations: Creep and cold flow under load
Little elastic recovery
Poor abrasion resistance in virgin form
Higher thermal expansion than metals

families.name: Compressed non-asbestos fibre (CNAF) sheet
families.description: Gasket sheet made from fibres (for example aramid, glass, carbon or mineral fibres) and fillers bound with an elastomer binder such as NBR and compressed into sheet. It replaced former asbestos-based sheets in water and general services and is often used for split-case casing joint gaskets cut to the joint shape.
families.mechanicalStrength: Good crush resistance over a useful sealing stress range. Performance depends on thickness, bolt load and flange stiffness; thinner gaskets generally relax less under load.
families.corrosionResistance: Depends on fibre and binder. Generally good in water, oils and many mild chemicals; limited in strong acids, strong alkalis and some solvents.
families.wearResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
families.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
families.temperatureSuitability: Moderate. The safe envelope is defined by the combination of pressure, temperature and thickness in the gasket manufacturer data; the binder ages at elevated temperature and in steam.
families.costConsiderations: Low.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Cut from sheet. For split-case joints the OEM specifies gasket material and thickness, because thickness affects the relative position of the casing halves, bore roundness and the clamping of wear rings and seal housings. Gaskets are not reused.
advantages: Low cost and easily cut to shape
Good sealing in water and oils
limitations: Pressure, temperature and thickness limits must be respected
Binder degrades at high temperature and in steam
Limited resistance to strong chemicals
Incorrect thickness alters internal fits in split-case pumps
suitableService: General industrial service at low to moderate pressure

families.name: Spiral wound gaskets
families.description: Semi-metallic gaskets made by winding a preformed metal strip (often stainless steel) together with a soft filler such as flexible graphite, PTFE or a mineral-based material, usually with an outer centring ring and often an inner ring. Used on circular bolted flanges at higher pressures and temperatures or where blow-out resistance is required.
families.mechanicalStrength: High resilience and blow-out resistance; needs adequate bolt load and a suitable flange surface finish.
families.corrosionResistance: Depends on the winding metal and filler, both of which must be compatible with the fluid.
families.wearResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
families.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
families.temperatureSuitability: High; limited by the filler and winding metal selected.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Manufactured to suit standard flange dimensions; not normally used on the irregular split joint of a casing. Must be handled carefully to avoid damaging or unwinding the spiral.
limitations: Needs high bolt load and stiff flanges
Unsuitable for irregular split-joint shapes
Easily damaged by poor handling
Single use
suitableService: Higher pressure or temperature nozzle flanges
typicalUse: Seal gland plate gaskets in some designs

families.name: Flexible (exfoliated) graphite
families.description: Expanded graphite formed into sheet, tape or rings. Used for gaskets (often with a metal reinforcing insert), as the filler of spiral wound gaskets, and as die-formed packing rings or braided graphite packing.
families.mechanicalStrength: Low strength on its own; reinforced sheets add handling strength. Conforms well to flange surfaces and shows low stress relaxation.
families.corrosionResistance: Wide chemical resistance except to strongly oxidising media. In the presence of an electrolyte it can promote galvanic corrosion of some metals, and low-impurity grades are used against stainless steel.
families.wearResistance: Self-lubricating when used as packing.
families.abrasionResistance: Limited; abrasive solids damage graphite packing.
families.temperatureSuitability: Very wide temperature range in inert or non-oxidising conditions; oxidises in air at high temperature.
families.costConsiderations: Moderate.
families.manufacturingConsiderations: Unreinforced sheet is fragile; reinforced variants are easier to cut and handle. Die-formed packing rings must be sized to the stuffing box.
limitations: Oxidises in air at high temperature
Attacked by strong oxidisers
Can promote galvanic corrosion of some metals
Fragile and easily damaged in handling

components.label: Suction, stage and discharge casings
components.selectionNotes: Pressure rating and temperature decide between irons and steels; corrosion decides between steel and stainless grades. Higher stage counts mean higher discharge pressure in the same casing family - check the casing pressure rating for the maximum discharge pressure, including shut-off.

components.label: Impellers
components.selectionNotes: High tip speed and erosion-corrosion favour 13Cr-4Ni or duplex in hot or treated water; bronze is economical in clean cold water.

components.label: Diffusers and return channels
components.selectionNotes: Usually the same family as the casing or the impeller; vane inlets erode first.

components.label: Shaft
components.selectionNotes: Strength and fatigue resistance for a long span; stainless where wetted or in corrosive service.

components.label: Shaft sleeves and interstage sleeves
components.selectionNotes: Wear and corrosion resistance; hardness difference to the mating bush where they run in close clearance.

components.label: Wear rings, interstage bushes, balance drum bush / disc seat
components.selectionNotes: Must resist galling with the rotating partner; dissimilar hardness or non-galling polymers are used. Polymer rings need OEM approval for temperature and liquid.

components.label: Bearings
components.selectionNotes: Rolling bearings in through-hardened bearing steel; large or high-speed pumps may use hydrodynamic sleeve and tilting-pad thrust bearings.

components.label: Mechanical seal faces
components.selectionNotes: Carbon vs silicon carbide is common for clean water; hard/hard pairs for abrasive liquids. Hot water needs face materials and cooling suited to poor lubricity.

components.label: Elastomers (O-rings, secondary seals)
components.selectionNotes: EPDM suits hot water and steam condensate but not mineral oils; NBR suits oils and cold water; FKM / FFKM for chemicals and higher temperatures.

components.label: Gaskets
components.selectionNotes: Joint design (gasket or O-ring) is set by the OEM; always use new gaskets.

components.label: Tie bolts and nuts
components.selectionNotes: High-strength alloy-steel studs and nuts (e.g. ASTM A193 B7 / A194 2H); stainless or coated bolting in corrosive atmospheres.

services.title: Clean water (supply, boosting, cooling water)
services.summary: Moderate temperature, low corrosivity, few solids. Economical materials are usually adequate.

factors.explanation: Discharge pressure grows with the stage count; ductile iron or steel casings may be needed for higher stage counts.
Chlorides, low pH or aggressive soft water can attack irons; check the water analysis.
Sand wears wear rings and bushes quickly; consider harder materials or filtration.

combinations.rationale: Economical, castable; ductile iron for higher pressure.
Bronze or stainless for corrosion and erosion resistance.

cautions: Potable water needs materials approved for drinking water by the local regulations.
No material choice is universal - check pressure, temperature and water analysis.

services.title: Boiler feedwater (hot, treated water)
services.summary: High temperature, high pressure, low oxygen; erosion-corrosion and thermal transients govern material choice.

factors.explanation: Casings must keep their pressure rating at temperature; warm-up procedures avoid distortion and rubbing in close clearances.
Plain carbon steel can thin at high velocity in some water chemistries; 13 % Cr steels resist it better.
pH control and oxygen removal (deaerator) strongly affect material life; upsets cause rapid damage.
Water near saturation needs suction head from an elevated deaerator or a booster pump.

combinations.rationale: Pressure and temperature capability; chromium steel against erosion-corrosion.
13Cr-4Ni type castings are widely used for hot feedwater stages.
Hardness difference or non-galling materials for hot running clearances.
Hot water / condensate compatible compounds; check temperature limits.

cautions: Seal cooling or a cooled flush is often required.
Temperature limits of each material and component come from the OEM and the applicable codes.

services.title: Chemical and process service
services.summary: Corrosion resistance and compatibility of every wetted material - including elastomers and seal faces - decide the selection.

factors.explanation: Acids, alkalis, chlorides, solvents and their concentration and temperature determine which alloys and elastomers survive.
Austenitic stainless steels can crack in hot chlorides; duplex grades resist better.
Toxic or flammable liquids need double seals with a barrier or buffer system; the standard (e.g. API 610) may apply.

combinations.rationale: Broad corrosion resistance; duplex for chlorides and strength.
Chemical resistance; FFKM for the most aggressive media.

cautions: Use corrosion data for the exact liquid, concentration and temperature; when in doubt, consult the OEM and material suppliers.
Small amounts of impurities (e.g. chlorides) can change the choice completely.

formulas.title: Flow rate from velocity
formulas.expression: Q = v x A = v x pi x d^2 / 4

variables.meaning: discharge / suction pressure at the nozzles

example.given: p_d - p_s = 27.5 bar, water 1000 kg/m3, velocity and height terms 0.3 m

formulas.title: Head per stage and total head
formulas.expression: H_total ~ n_st x H_stage ;  H_stage = H_total / n_st
formulas.notes: The same flow passes all stages. Stage heads are similar but not identical (first and last stages, leakage).

formulas.title: Number of stages

variables.meaning: head per stage available from the chosen impeller at the duty flow

formulas.notes: Round UP; the impeller diameter may then be trimmed (or one stage fitted with a reduced impeller) to meet the duty without excess head.

formulas.title: Hydraulic (output) power
formulas.expression: P_h = rho x g x Q x H

formulas.title: Motor input (electrical) power
formulas.notes: Motor rating is chosen with a margin above the maximum shaft power on the curve (e.g. at the end of the allowable region) - margins come from the specification / standard.

formulas.title: Pump efficiency
formulas.expression: eta_p = P_h / P = rho g Q H / P

formulas.title: Shaft torque
formulas.expression: T = P / omega = 60 x P / (2 pi n)

formulas.expression: NPSHa = (p_s,abs - p_v) / (rho g) + v_s^2 / (2 g) ;  margin = NPSHa / NPSHr (or NPSHa - NPSHr)

maintenance.title: Casing disassembly (NDE first)
maintenance.purpose: Open the pump from the non-drive end to reach the stages.
steps: Remove coupling guard and spacer; record alignment.
Drain oil, remove NDE bearing housing and bearing.
Remove NDE shaft nut, seal, sleeve and seal chamber (seal setting clips fitted).
Remove discharge cover and the balance drum (or disc) and its bush (or seat).
inspectionPoints: Balance drum/bush clearance or disc faces - measure before cleaning.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.
commonMistakes: Not recording the as-found alignment and rotor axial position.
Losing the order / orientation of parts.

maintenance.title: Tie-bolt removal
tools: Torque wrench or hydraulic tensioner (as the OEM specifies)
steps: Support the casing sections.
Mark all sections in order and orientation.
Slacken the tie-bolt nuts gradually in a crossing pattern; withdraw the bolts.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.
commonMistakes: Releasing one bolt fully while others are tight.
Not supporting the sections so that they drop on the rotor.

maintenance.title: Stage-by-stage impeller removal
maintenance.purpose: Remove discharge casing, impellers and ring sections in order.
tools: Heating equipment if the impellers are shrink-fitted (OEM procedure)
steps: Slide off the discharge casing (with the last diffuser).
Pull the last impeller and its key.
Slide off the next ring section with its diffuser, return channel and bush.
Repeat stage by stage to the first impeller.
inspectionPoints: Each impeller, diffuser, wear ring and bush - measure clearances.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.
commonMistakes: Levering on vanes or wear-ring lands.

maintenance.title: Shaft and bearing inspection
maintenance.purpose: Confirm the shaft and bearings can be reused.
steps: Measure run-out along the shaft.
Inspect seats, keyways, threads, journals.
Inspect bearings; replace rolling bearings removed with pullers unless the OEM states otherwise.
inspectionPoints: Run-out, journal diameters, fretting, cracks at stress raisers.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.
commonMistakes: Supporting the long shaft at only two points (sag).

maintenance.title: Mechanical seal installation
maintenance.purpose: Fit the seals correctly so that they start without leaking.
steps: Clean sleeve, chamber and faces.
Fit the seal (cartridge: as a unit; component seal: set the working length).
Bolt the gland evenly; remove the setting clips only after the rotor is fully clamped and positioned.
inspectionPoints: Sleeve surface, chamber bore and face squareness.
safety: Faces are brittle - do not drop.
commonMistakes: Touching seal faces with bare fingers.

maintenance.title: Stage assembly
maintenance.purpose: Rebuild the stage stack in the correct order with correct clearances.
steps: Fit impeller 1 and key against the stop.
Fit ring section 1 with diffuser, return channel and bush; then interstage sleeve and impeller 2.
Repeat; finish with the discharge casing.
Check rotor axial position and float at the stage indicated by the OEM.
inspectionPoints: Clearances within limits; each impeller centred in its diffuser.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.

maintenance.title: Interstage gasket installation
tools: New gaskets / O-rings of the specified material and thickness
steps: Clean faces and spigots; fit new gasket or O-ring; do not use jointing compound unless specified.
Assemble the ring squarely without damaging the gasket.
commonMistakes: Using a different thickness (changes rotor position in some designs).

maintenance.title: Alignment checks
tools: Laser alignment system or dial indicators
steps: Check and correct soft foot.
Align the motor to the pump (pump is fixed to the piping).
Re-check after piping is connected; for hot pumps follow the OEM hot/cold offsets.
inspectionPoints: Offset and angularity within OEM / coupling limits.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.
commonMistakes: Aligning before the piping is connected.
Ignoring thermal growth in hot service.

maintenance.title: Final assembly inspection and first start
maintenance.purpose: Confirm the pump is safe to start.
steps: Rotor turns freely by hand.
Oil levels, seal flush, balance line open, valves set.
Fill and vent completely; start against a partly open discharge valve / minimum-flow line as the OEM specifies.
Record pressures, flow, power, vibration and bearing temperatures.
inspectionPoints: Leak-free joints and seals, bearing temperatures stabilise, balance leak-off normal.
safety: Lock out / tag out the driver; isolate, depressurise, drain and vent (including the balance line).
Let hot pumps cool; hot water flashes to steam when released.
Use rated lifting gear; ring sections and rotors are heavy and can roll.

failures.title: Cavitation
symptoms: Crackling noise at the suction end
causes: NPSHa too low (low suction level, blocked strainer, hot liquid)
Air or vapour in the suction

Inspect first-stage impeller

failures.title: Insufficient discharge pressure
symptoms: Flow too high or too low for the system
inspection: Check speed and rotation
Measure leak-off flow
Compare power and head with the curve

failures.title: Excessive axial thrust
inspection: Balance-chamber pressure
Leak-off flow trend
Thrust-bearing temperature
prevention: Keep leak-off line open; trend it

failures.title: Balance disc / drum failure
inspection: Measure clearances / face wear
Check rotor axial position
corrective: Recondition or renew in matched pairs

failures.title: Bearing overheating
inspection: Oil level and analysis
Alignment
Thrust conditions

failures.title: Mechanical seal leakage
inspection: Seal faces and O-rings
Flush flow and temperature

failures.title: Shaft failure
inspection: Fracture surface (beach marks)
Alignment and run-out history

failures.title: Impeller erosion
inspection: Vane thickness, shroud condition

failures.title: Interstage leakage
inspection: Clearance measurement at overhaul
Performance test
prevention: Avoid off-design operation and dry running

failures.title: Excessive vibration
causes: Operation near a critical speed or far from BEP
inspection: Vibration spectrum (1x, 2x, vane-pass)
Alignment
Soft foot

failures.title: Misalignment

Soft-foot check
Pipe-strain check
