inspection: Flow and temperature rise
Minimum-flow line operation

standards.fullTitle: Technical specifications for centrifugal pumps — Class II
standards.edition: 2002 edition, published 2002-03-14. It replaced ISO 5199:1986, which is withdrawn. No amendment was found in the ISO catalogue data checked. Adopted in Europe as EN ISO 5199:2002.
standards.status: Published (current). The ISO catalogue data show the systematic review at stage 90.60 "Close of review", dated 2023-06-05. No revision project was found.
standards.technicalScope:
ISO 5199 sets Class II technical requirements for centrifugal pumps for general application. That covers single-stage and multistage pumps, horizontal and vertical, with any type of drive and any installation arrangement. It was written with chemical-process pumps (for example those built to ISO 2858 dimensions) as typical examples, but it is not limited to them.

It deals with the design features that affect installation, maintenance and safe operation of the pump unit, including the baseplate, the coupling and the auxiliary piping. It also covers materials, shop inspection and testing, and the information that passes between purchaser and supplier, including a pump data sheet. The driver is outside its scope except for its rated power output. A supplier may offer a pump that does not meet every requirement, as long as each deviation is declared in the offer.
standards.applicability: ISO 5199 covers single-stage and multistage centrifugal pumps, so it can be used as the Class II specification for a general-industry ring-section pump by agreement in the purchase order. In this module it is the reference for general expectations on casing, shaft, bearings, seals, coupling, baseplate and documentation. Hydraulic acceptance testing is specified separately (ISO 9906).
standards.limitations:
Being a split case pump does not make a pump compliant with ISO 5199, and neither does a mention of the standard in a catalogue. Conformance has to be written into the purchase specification. The data sheet must be completed, the supplier must declare any deviations and the purchaser must accept them, and compliance must be shown through the documents, inspections and tests the order requires.

ISO 5199 is a Class II specification. For more severe services, such as petroleum, petrochemical or natural gas process duty, the purchaser may require API 610 or ISO 13709 instead. This module only summarises the purpose of the standard. It does not reproduce its requirements, values or text, which are copyright of ISO, so always work from the purchased current edition.
standards.verificationNote: Checked online on 2026-11-06, but not on iso.org itself: iso.org returned HTTP 403 to automated access. The reference, title, publication date (2002-03-14), owner committee (ISO/TC 115/SC 1), withdrawn predecessor and review stage come from ISO catalogue records (ISO project 31945) republished by two ISO national members, the Institute for Standardization of Montenegro and the General Directorate of Standardization of Albania. A search-engine index of iso.org confirmed the page title and URL. Those records show no confirm/revise decision after the review closed in June 2023. Open the iso.org page in a browser before publication to confirm the status and check whether a revision has started.

standards.fullTitle: Rotodynamic pumps — Hydraulic performance acceptance tests — Grades 1, 2 and 3
standards.edition: 2012 edition, published 2012-04-26. It replaced ISO 9906:1999 (now withdrawn), which covered Grades 1 and 2 only. No amendment was found in the ISO catalogue data checked. Adopted in Europe as EN ISO 9906:2012.
standards.status: Published (current). The ISO catalogue data show the systematic review at stage 90.60 "Close of review", dated 2022-12-03. No revision project was found.
standards.technicalScope:
ISO 9906 defines the hydraulic performance tests used when a customer accepts a rotodynamic pump (centrifugal, mixed-flow or axial) of any size. The test liquid must behave like clean cold water. The tests are meant to be run at a pump test facility, such as the manufacturer's works or an independent laboratory. They can be run on the bare pump or with some or all of its inlet and outlet fittings in place.

The standard covers which quantities are measured (flow rate, pump total head, power input and efficiency, and NPSH), the measurement methods and their uncertainty, the test arrangements, and how test results are converted to the guarantee conditions. It defines three acceptance grades: Grade 1 has the narrowest tolerances and Grade 3 the widest. Sub-grades with letter suffixes (B, E, U) set how the tolerance band is applied around the guarantee point.
standards.applicability: The usual international reference for the factory performance test of a multistage pump: flow, total head, power, efficiency and, if specified, NPSH3 of the first stage. The grade is chosen in the order.
standards.limitations:
Passing an ISO 9906 test shows that the pump met the agreed hydraulic guarantees on a test stand with clean cold water. It does not show mechanical integrity, vibration, or seal and bearing behaviour. It also does not show performance in the installed system, where inlet conditions and fluid properties are different. Field tests are generally less accurate than shop tests and cannot directly replace them. The standard does not apply automatically: the order must state the grade, guarantee points, witness requirements and test procedure.

Tolerance values, formulae and tables are not reproduced here. Use the purchased current edition, which is copyright of ISO.
standards.verificationNote: Checked online on 2026-11-06, but not on iso.org itself: iso.org returned HTTP 403 to automated access. The reference, title, publication date (2012-04-26), owner committee (ISO/TC 115/SC 2), withdrawn predecessor (ISO 9906:1999) and review stage come from ISO catalogue records (ISO project 41202) republished by the Institute for Standardization of Montenegro. The Standards Council of Canada and AFNOR listings agree. Those records show no confirm/revise decision after the review closed in December 2022. Open the iso.org page in a browser before publication to confirm the status.

standards.fullTitle: Rotodynamic Pumps for Hydraulic Performance Acceptance Tests
standards.edition: 2022 edition. It supersedes ANSI/HI 14.6-2016, and HI's version history also lists earlier editions (2011, 2000).
standards.status: Current. The Hydraulic Institute product page marks it as the current version and mentions no newer edition or revision in progress.
standards.technicalScope: HI 14.6 sets out how rotodynamic pumps (centrifugal, mixed-flow and axial-flow) are tested and accepted. It covers four test types: hydraulic performance, NPSH, hydrostatic pressure and mechanical integrity. It also covers instrumentation, test arrangements and procedures, and the acceptance criteria for the results. Acceptance uses three grade levels with different tolerance bands and measurement-accuracy demands. The grade structure parallels the one in ISO 9906.
standards.applicability: North American equivalent reference for hydraulic acceptance tests of rotodynamic pumps, including multistage pumps.
standards.limitations: A pump has only been tested to HI 14.6 if the test was ordered, carried out and reported to the standard at the agreed grade. A catalogue curve is not an acceptance test. Shop tests use clean cold water and the test stand's own piping, so installed performance can be different. HI standards are copyright publications. This module only paraphrases their purpose and does not reproduce tolerances, tables or text.
standards.verificationNote: Verified on 2026-11-06 on the Hydraulic Institute product page (pumps.org). The page marks this as the current version, says it supersedes the 2016 edition, and HI's standards listing shows 2022 for this title. The HI page gives no ANSI approval date, and the ANSI Webstore returned HTTP 403, so that date is not verified. The statement that the grade structure parallels ISO 9906 is based on HI's published descriptions. Check it, and any changes made in 2022, against the purchased edition.

standards.edition: 2022 edition. It supersedes ANSI/HI 9.6.6-2016; the earlier edition was 2009.
standards.status: Current. The Hydraulic Institute product page marks it as the current version.
standards.technicalScope:
HI 9.6.6 covers the piping immediately upstream and downstream of rotodynamic pumps and how that piping affects pump performance and reliability. On the inlet side it deals with pipe size and velocity, swirl generated by the piping, minimum straight pipe lengths after fittings that disturb the flow, and suction elbows, including their orientation at double-suction pumps. It also says when a physical model study or CFD is appropriate. On the outlet side it covers piping, valves and water hammer. For both sides it covers pipe-to-nozzle alignment and nozzle loads, pipe supports, anchors and expansion joints, and parallel operation. A final part explains how to assess and fix existing piping that does not conform.

It does not cover piping that discharges into tanks, vessels or intake structures. Intake design is covered by ANSI/HI 9.8.
standards.applicability: Suction and discharge piping guidance - important for the first stage of a multistage pump (NPSH, inflow quality).
standards.limitations: Following the principles of the standard does not guarantee good pump inlet conditions on every site. Unusual layouts may need a model study or a review by the manufacturer. Straight-length numbers and other requirements depend on the fitting type, the pump type and the suction energy, so read them from the purchased current edition. This module gives no numeric values and reproduces no HI text. Conformance only applies where a project specification calls up the standard and the as-built piping is checked against it.
standards.verificationNote: Verified on 2026-11-06 in two places on the HI site. The product page (pumps.org) marks it as the current version and says it supersedes the 2016 edition. HI's public table of contents (pumps.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/9.6.6-Table-of-Contents.pdf, copyright 1997–2022) confirms the 2022 content outline, including the figures on elbows at double-suction pumps. The exact approval or publication date is not on the HI page. A reseller gives a 2022 publication date and the same ISBN, but HI has not confirmed the date.

standards.fullTitle: Rotodynamic Pumps - Guideline for Operating Regions
standards.edition: 2024 edition (table of contents dated January 2024); supersedes the 2018 edition.
standards.status: Current according to the Hydraulic Institute product page checked on 2026-11-06.
standards.technicalScope: Preferred operating region (POR, based on specific speed) and allowable operating region (AOR), the factors that define them, and the effect of the operating point on reliability and efficiency.
standards.applicability: Explains why a multistage pump should run near BEP and why low-flow operation needs a minimum-flow arrangement.
standards.limitations: A guideline; the AOR of a specific pump is stated by its manufacturer. Text and values are not reproduced here.
standards.verificationNote: Edition and supersession taken from pumps.org search results and the HI table-of-contents PDF (pumps.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/TOC-9.6.3-2024.pdf). Open the product page to confirm before publishing.

standards.organisation: API (American Petroleum Institute); ISO for ISO 13709
standards.fullTitle: Centrifugal Pumps for Petroleum, Petrochemical, and Natural Gas Industries (API Std 610); Centrifugal pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries (ISO 13709)
standards.edition: 13th edition, published June 2026 (reported by Hydrocarbon Processing, Aug 2026, and listed by BSI Knowledge as API STD 610:2026, 29 Jun 2026). The 12th edition (2021) is superseded.
standards.status: Current according to secondary sources checked on 2026-11-06; the API catalogue page was not read directly.
standards.technicalScope:
API 610 specifies requirements for centrifugal pumps used in petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry process services, including pumps run in reverse as hydraulic power recovery turbines. It classifies pumps by configuration: overhung (OH), between-bearings (BB) and vertically suspended (VS). A single-stage, axially split, between-bearings pump is the BB1 type. The standard sets requirements for design, pressure casings, rotors and rotordynamics, and for bearings and lubrication. It covers shaft sealing, with mechanical seals generally specified to API 682, as well as couplings, baseplates and auxiliary piping. It also covers materials, inspection and testing (including performance, NPSH and vibration acceptance), data sheets and documentation.

According to trade press (not the standard itself), the 13th Edition revises rotordynamics, casing pressure rating and joint bolting, seal chamber dimensions, NPSH reference points and margin, auxiliary piping connections, coupling sizing and baseplate requirements.
standards.applicability: Applies when the purchaser specifies it, typically for petroleum, petrochemical and natural-gas service. API 610 classifies between-bearings multistage pumps by casing type: BB3 (axially split multistage), BB4 (single-casing radially split multistage - the ring-section type shown here) and BB5 (double-casing, barrel). A general water-service ring-section pump is usually not an API 610 pump; never assume compliance.
standards.limitations: An axially split double-suction pump is not an API 610 pump because of its configuration. Compliance requires the specification to call up a stated edition, the data sheets to be completed, exceptions to be listed and agreed, and compliance to be demonstrated by inspection, test and documentation. The specification must also state which document applies, because API 610 13th Edition and ISO 13709:2009 are no longer technically identical. Projects still working to the 11th or 12th Edition must say so. Requirements change between editions, so do not assume that a clause in one edition exists in another. No API or ISO text is reproduced here.
standards.verificationNote: Hydrocarbon Processing news item (Aug 2026) "API 610 thirteenth edition is now available" and BSI Knowledge listing. Confirm the edition and the ISO 13709 relationship in the API publications catalogue before publishing; the ISO 13709 equivalence of the 13th edition was not confirmed.

quiz.question: Which part converts the high velocity leaving each impeller into pressure in this pump?
quiz.explanation: Ring-section multistage pumps use a vaned diffuser around each impeller; volutes are typical of single-stage pumps.

quiz.question: In a 5-stage pump, the flow through stage 3 is ...
options: one fifth of the pump flow
the same as the pump flow
quiz.explanation: Stages are in series: the same flow passes through every stage while the heads add up.

quiz.question: What holds the suction casing, ring sections and discharge casing together?
quiz.explanation: Tie bolts clamp the stack; their preload keeps the joints closed under pressure.

quiz.question: What leads the liquid from one stage to the eye of the next impeller?
quiz.explanation: Return vanes guide the flow inward and remove swirl before the next eye.

quiz.question: Why are multistage pumps used?
options: For very high flow at low head
For high head at moderate flow
quiz.explanation: Stages in series multiply the head at the same flow.

quiz.question: Where is the pressure lowest in the pump?
quiz.explanation: The first-stage eye sees suction pressure minus the inlet losses - this is where cavitation starts.

quiz.question: When reassembling ring sections, the joint gaskets should be ...
options: replaced with new ones of the specified type
left out if the faces are good
quiz.explanation: Gaskets and O-rings are always renewed; type and thickness as specified by the OEM.

quiz.question: Which part turns with the shaft?
quiz.explanation: Interstage sleeves are part of the rotor stack between impellers; the bush around them is stationary.

quiz.question: A duty needs 300 m; one stage gives 70 m at the duty flow. How many stages?
quiz.explanation: 300 / 70 = 4.29 -> round up to 5 stages, then trim the impellers to avoid excess head.

quiz.question: Q = 60 m3/h, H = 280 m, water, eta = 70 %. Shaft power is about ...
Why do the impeller axial forces add up in this pump?
options: Because all impellers face the same direction
quiz.explanation: In-line impellers all push toward their suction eyes, i.e. toward the suction end.

quiz.question: The balance chamber behind the drum is connected to ...
quiz.explanation: The leak-off line keeps the chamber near suction pressure, creating the pressure difference across the drum.

quiz.question: Speed is reduced from 2950 to 2500 rpm. The head becomes about ...
Discharge pressure has slowly fallen over two years and power per unit flow has risen. Most likely cause?
options: Worn wear rings and interstage bushes
quiz.explanation: Clearance wear increases internal leakage - the classic slow decline of a multistage pump.

quiz.question: For hot boiler feedwater impellers, a commonly used material family is ...
quiz.explanation: It resists erosion-corrosion in hot treated water and has high strength; selection still depends on the water chemistry and OEM.

quiz.question: Specific speed of a multistage pump is calculated with ...
quiz.explanation: n_q uses head per stage (and flow per eye).

quiz.question: With a balance disc, why do both bearings have to allow axial movement?
options: Because the disc itself positions the rotor axially
quiz.explanation: The disc finds its own equilibrium gap; a locating thrust bearing would fight it.

quiz.question: The NDE thrust-bearing temperature rises while flow and head are normal (drum design). First check?
options: Balance (leak-off) line open and balance-chamber pressure
quiz.explanation: A restricted leak-off raises balance-chamber pressure, reducing the drum force and overloading the thrust bearing.

quiz.question: Why can worn annular clearances increase vibration in a long multistage rotor?
options: The liquid films in tight clearances add stiffness and damping (Lomakin effect); wear reduces it
quiz.explanation: Annular seals act like hydrodynamic bearings along the rotor; larger clearances give less support, lowering the wet critical speed and damping.

quiz.question: Which statement about balancing methods is correct?
options: A drum balances thrust automatically at every operating point
A disc usually needs a large thrust bearing
Opposed impellers reduce net thrust but need crossover passages
Balance holes are the standard for multistage boiler feed pumps
quiz.explanation: Opposed (back-to-back) groups largely cancel thrust at the cost of crossover passages and casing complexity.

quiz.question: A boiler feed pump is run for a long time with the discharge valve closed and no minimum-flow line. Likely result?
options: Liquid heats up, may flash; seal, balance device and clearances can be damaged
Lower motor current and no risk
quiz.explanation: Almost all power turns into heat in very little liquid; hot feedwater is close to saturation.

quiz.question: NPSHa = 15.3 m, NPSHr (NPSH3) = 3.2 m at the duty point. Which statement is right?
options: Ratio 4.8: generous margin; still check the OEM margin and the whole flow range
NPSHr must be added to the head
quiz.explanation: NPSH3 already implies a 3 % head drop; margins are judged against OEM / ANSI/HI 9.6.1 guidance over the operating range.

quiz.question: Why is the NDE mechanical seal of a drum-balanced ring-section pump not exposed to full discharge pressure?
options: It is behind the balance chamber, which is held near suction pressure
Because it is a double seal
It is exposed to full discharge pressure
quiz.explanation: The drum throttles discharge pressure down to balance-chamber pressure before the seal.

quiz.question: During reassembly, when should the mechanical seal setting clips be removed?
options: After the rotor stack is clamped and its axial position set
quiz.explanation: The seal working length is only correct once the rotor is in its final axial position.
